items.caption:
Higgsfield founder Alex Mashrabov says the company launches new products pretty much every week, and that speed makes customer support with AI agents harder.

The agents are only as good as the context and rules they are given, so when those change about twice a week, a smart, coordinated team has to keep updating the agents and playbooks.

Full conversation: 20VC with Harry Stebbings and Alex Mashrabov, founder of Higgsfield.

items.caption:
Swipe to see the a16z-backed startup Salesforce reportedly just bought.

Rune Technologies builds AI software that helps the US military forecast what supplies troops will need and manage logistics out in the field.

Salesforce has agreed to acquire Rune for $375 million in cash and stock, Resilience Media reported. Founded in 2024, Rune raised $30 million in total from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures and IQT, and was last valued at $127 million after a Series A led by Human Capital, according to PitchBook.

The deal plugs Rune into Missionforce, the Salesforce unit that sells to defense and national security agencies. Salesforce says Missionforce grew 80% year over year, helped by a new 10-year, $5.6 billion contract with the US Army. Rune's data would take it from back-office planning to battlefield operations. It is the latest in a busy year of Salesforce deals, after Fin ($3.6 billion) and Qualified ($1.2 billion).

Sources: TechCrunch, Resilience Media.

Sam Altman says that at Stanford, "for no reason, other than peer pressure", he went after an investment banking internship and got one, because that was what the smartest kids were chasing.

The New York interview and fancy dinner impressed him at 18 or 19, but a growing feeling of dread followed. Then Y Combinator offered money to live on for the summer to try a startup with the project he was building with friends, and he took it as a sign.

Source: Stanford GSB, View From The Top with Sam Altman (co-founder and CEO of OpenAI). Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=anAmTGcewX8

items.caption:
Swipe to see the AI startup trying to buy a famous law firm's name.

Crosby is an AI-first law firm. Instead of selling legal AI software to other firms, it is a licensed firm itself and uses its own AI to deliver legal work faster.

Congrats @crosbylegal

The two-year-old firm has put in a bid for some of Weil Gotshal's assets, including its trademark, its brand and some internal data, TechCrunch confirmed after The Information first reported it. Weil Gotshal, a once-prestigious Wall Street firm, told the New York Times it is preparing to vote on dissolving. Crosby is also working to hire some of its 1,200 lawyers. Terms weren't disclosed, and there's no guarantee Crosby wins.

Crosby has raised about $85 million, including a $60 million Series B in March led by Lux and Index, with Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors and Bain Capital Ventures also in. It came out of stealth in 2025 with a $5.8 million seed.

Sources: TechCrunch, The Information.

items.caption:
Swipe to see the startup that picks your next restaurant from where you've actually eaten.

Zest connects to your credit card through Plaid, looks only at food and drink purchases, and uses them to learn your taste. Its new AI concierge works over plain text: ask for a cuisine, a neighborhood or an occasion, and it suggests spots and books the table through OpenTable, Resy or SevenRooms.

Congrats @zestmaps

Drop it into a group chat and it blends everyone's tastes, runs a vote in the thread, and books for the group. "The agent is the product now," founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall told TechCrunch. Booking and ordering are its first ways to make money.

Zest was founded in November 2024 with $1.8 million in pre-seed funding from Alexis Ohanian's 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, and wants to grow beyond its first few thousand users.

Sources: TechCrunch, Zest.
